subject: mckenna-grace
research_tasks: Open the long-form sit-down material from the Sunrise on the Reaping press tour (US release 2026-11-20): podcasts or profiles of 30+ minutes, not red-carpet junkets. Code every adult account of a setback by her response: reassurance, preparation and trusted people (6); re-asserting image and output (3); reframing toward fun or new options (7); turning toward others' needs (2). Candidate setbacks: losing the Scream 7 role she first auditioned for (S02, S20), the year of pulled music releases (C18), the 2026 'internet hates you' cycle (C19).

Find named, on-record testimony from adult-era collaborators who are not promoting a joint project with her or dating her: Francis Lawrence, Josh Boone, Kevin Williamson, Emma Tammi, Allison Williams or Dave Franco as Regretting You producers, the Scooby-Doo: Origins showrunners. Look for how she takes notes, criticism and pressure, not for praise of her work ethic.

Identify the 2026 online backlash she referenced to THR (2026-03-07: 'Every other week, the internet either loves you or hates you') and SiriusXM (June 2026: 'they kind of decide when they like you and they don't'). Establish what happened and her own adult response from dated primary posts or interviews.

Get a second, independent first-person account of the roughly year-long run of pulled music releases, and of what finally let her release 'Ugly and Rotten' (June 2026) and 'Bones and All' (2026-09-25): reassurance from trusted people (6), a strategic or schedule decision (3), or something else.

Find an adult interview, outside junket framing, where she weighs a small part in a franchise she loves against a lead elsewhere, or explains turning work down. This tests whether the role-size answer (C16) holds as a discriminator against Three.

Test the Two alternative. Find adult evidence of what she does when relationships and work conflict (time with family or Mason Thames against bookings), and whether her caretaking (C25) extends beyond the cast 'families' she belongs to.

Before any direct quotation, re-transcribe from audio (Whisper large-v3-turbo) the auto-caption passages relied on here: SiriusXM DaGfC6UwbCo 15:09-15:45 and 01:00-01:45; ET whkWpbfsFmg 02:48-04:30; Who Let Alyssa Out igfn1lbEL6o 04:07-05:30; Collider s56VU0CWnfA 12:38-13:45 and 30:25-31:10. YouTube audio downloads returned HTTP 403 on 2026-10-27, so only captions were read.

Keep minor-era material out of the type argument; she turned 18 on 2024-06-25. Deliberately not used: PAPER (2022-07-08), NME on 'Self Dysmorphia' (2023), Zach Sang (2023-10-19), Consequence (2024-01-08), Riff Magazine (age 17), Bob Saget's Here For You (2021), and the 2024-06-02 JackManifold stream. Do not convert this to an open case. Her public career began around 2012 (Crash & Bernstein) and her breakout was Gifted (2017), so she fails the standard's early-public-career rule. sources.title: Mckenna Grace, Relentless Optimist (Teen Vogue New Hollywood Class of 2025 cover; page title: 'Mckenna Grace Reveals Secret Hunger Games Edits and How She Landed Maysilee Donner')
sources.speaker: Mckenna Grace, interviewed by P. Claire Dodson; Teen Vogue
sources.locator: Full article. Key passages: opening ('There is little that... Grace can't spin into something good'); 'It is tiring at times, but I dig it'; mother's spreadsheet; 'gaslight myself into being happy or energetic'; 'Kindness... to a fault'; Troop Zero 'personality for a year'; 'The whole basis of my job is hoping that people like me'; closing section on work ethic ('Sometimes I feel like I do extra work because this industry is so cutthroat').
sources.excerpt: “It is tiring at times, but I dig it... Grass is always greener. I'd rather be doing 20 million things at once than just sitting at home and being like, 'Shoot. When can I get back to work?'” ... “It sounds really terrible when I put it this way... but I feel like some days I just gaslight myself into being happy or energetic.” ... “Kindness... I always want to make people feel important and seen. Even sometimes, maybe to a fault. I think that I can be a little overly excited.” ... “The whole basis of my job is hoping that people like me and that people want to hire me, or that the public likes my work.” ... “Sometimes I feel like I do extra work because this industry is so cutthroat at times... Of course, I put my career at very high importance, but I wouldn't want to put that over somebody else's expense, or step on somebody else to make my way up. It scares me, and I don't think I would like myself very much if that's who I became, or if that's who I let this industry make me.”
sources.context: The longest adult-era profile found, from a sit-down at her New York hotel during the Regretting You press week after a 20-hour trip from the Sunrise on the Reaping set (she was 19). Mixes direct quotation with the writer's framing ('Relentless Optimist'; she was 'searching for a bright side'), and the writer's observations are kept separate from her words. Also reports her mother travels with her and keeps a spreadsheet of projects, her Grapevine, Texas birthplace, the move to LA at five while her father finished medical school, and the paraphrased conversation with her mother about why she works so much. Childhood material appears only as her adult retrospection. Opened in full on 2026-10-27 via the r.jina.ai reader, because WebSearch is blocked from teenvogue.com. Promotional context: a magazine cover tied to Regretting You. Adult-era source (she turned 18 on 2024-06-25).

sources.title: Mckenna Grace Breaks Down Her Big 'Scream 7' Scene
sources.speaker: Mckenna Grace, interviewed by The Hollywood Reporter
sources.locator: Intro section and Q&A. Key answers: role size ('Not really. I mean, I don't even see myself that way'); Five Nights at Freddy's video to Scott Cawthon and Emma Tammi; virality ('I have never gotten nervous on a carpet or in interviews until now'); fan-base research ('So I always get very nervous and try to do my research'); stunt-team cookies; 'dream job' disingenuousness; pitching songs at video village; 'jeepers'.
sources.excerpt: “Not really. I mean, I don't even see myself that way. I don't even think that I could. I'm just so grateful for work. Am I going to turn down Five Nights at Freddy's 2? Am I going to turn down the chance of being in my favorite franchises? No. If I'm going to be there for five minutes, why not? That's so fun... All I've ever wanted is to work. I've been doing it since I was five.” ... “I will literally play a pair of shoes in the background of a scene. I would be so honored to be a part of this in any way. I would even be your shadow on set.” So I'm just a fan. ... “In that time, I have never gotten nervous on a carpet or in interviews until now. I did one interview at the Scream 7 premiere, and when I walked off of that carpet, I was a nervous wreck... Every other week, the internet either loves you or hates you.” ... “So I always get very nervous and try to do my research so I can perform to the best of my abilities without getting in my head about it.”
sources.context: Long post-release Q&A about Scream 7 (a franchise-best $64M domestic opening, per THR), done while she was at a convention. The interviewer explicitly put the status question to her: as a lead actor, would she hold out for leads? That makes her answer on role size the closest thing to a discriminating observation in the record. Also confirms she auditioned for another Scream 7 character before being cast as Hannah Thurman (THR surmises it was Tatum), that she did most of her own wire work after spinal surgery, and that 'Twisting the Knife' with Ice Nine Kills topped Billboard's hard rock chart. The byline was not captured by the reader. Opened in full on 2026-10-27 via r.jina.ai. She was 19. Adult-era source (she turned 18 on 2024-06-25).

sources.title: Mckenna Grace on Stepping Into a New Creative Chapter—And Her 20s
sources.speaker: Mckenna Grace, interviewed by Samantha Simon; L'OFFICIEL USA
sources.locator: Intro and full Q&A: 'Ugly and Rotten' origin; 'I don't like to not work'; work-life balance answer ('My job is my life'); Scooby-Doo impostor syndrome; Mason and her mother on her personality changing after each set; style and spinal surgery; turning-20 answer ('I treat every project like it could be my last').
sources.excerpt: “It's hard to find a work-life balance, but luckily I love my job. My job is my life. So it's like, this is all I do. I don't like to sit still, so I spend my weekends in the studio.” ... “I have the craziest impostor syndrome, but it's been so cool.” ... “They were like, Your personality changes a bit after each of the sets that you're on.” ... “In acting, I'm telling other people's stories. In music, I get to tell my own. It's a lot scarier... I find that I get to be a lot angrier or messier... When I'm singing, I don't want to feel like I'm putting on another identity, since that's what I do for work already.” ... “I'm on my dream job right now, and I treat every project like it could be my last. I don't want to get too ambitious; I just want to keep working, putting things out there that I can be proud of, and spending time with the people that I love.”
sources.context: Music-focused print Q&A, done on her way to the Scooby-Doo: Origins set in Atlanta hours after 'Ugly and Rotten' came out, weeks before her 20th birthday. It is the most reflective adult self-description in the record. She reports Mason Thames and her mother observing that her personality changes with each role. She also says she hasn't released music 'in over a year', has 'the craziest impostor syndrome', and has crossed the Oscars off her bucket list. Opened in full on 2026-10-27 via r.jina.ai (the publisher's HTML carries only a teaser). Adult-era source (she turned 18 on 2024-06-25).

claims.claim: Mckenna Grace was born on June 25, 2006, in Grapevine, Texas; she turned 20 in June 2026.
claims.inference: Birth date fixes the adult-era boundary (2024-06-25) used to select type evidence.
claims.alternative: None material; birthplace is from Teen Vogue's profile, birth date from Wikipedia's infobox.

claims.claim: She started acting as a small child. She begged for acting classes, and she and her mother flew to Los Angeles when she was five while her father finished medical school. Her father is a doctor and no one in her family works in entertainment.
claims.inference: Her career is a family project begun in early childhood; work has been the frame of her life since before she could choose it.
claims.alternative: This shapes how much of her work rate is temperament versus upbringing; it is circumstance, not type evidence.

claims.claim: Her mother travels with her and keeps a spreadsheet tracking all of her projects. In December 2024 her mother called her 'chronically online', after which she capped her TikTok use at about 30 minutes a day.
claims.inference: A close parental support structure still organizes her working life at 19-20.
claims.alternative: Ordinary for a young performer whose career began at five; does not by itself indicate a dependent or security-seeking temperament.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck if a profile reports a change in who manages or travels with her.

claims.claim: She was homeschooled and never attended a regular school.
claims.inference: Her peer world from childhood was film sets, which helps explain why casts become her 'families'.
claims.alternative: Background fact only.

claims.claim: Her music career: signed with Photo Finish Records in 2020, debut single 'Haunted House' in 2021 (on the Ghostbusters: Afterlife soundtrack), EPs in 2023, 'Twisting the Knife' with Ice Nine Kills for Scream 7 (topped Billboard's hard rock chart), 'Ugly and Rotten' in June 2026, 'Bones and All' on September 25, 2026.
claims.inference: Music is a sustained second career that she describes as the one place she tells her own story.
claims.alternative: Chart claim is THR's; label and early discography are Wikipedia's.

claims.claim: Recent and upcoming work: Regretting You (October 24, 2025; also executive producer), Five Nights at Freddy's 2 (December 2025), Scream 7 (February 27, 2026, as Hannah Thurman), Nimrods (US release August 14, 2026), The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (US release November 20, 2026, as Maysilee Donner and her twin Merrilee), and Netflix's Scooby-Doo: Origins (2027, eight episodes, as Daphne Blake).
claims.inference: Situates the November 2026 search spike and shows the density of her 2025-2026 output.
claims.alternative: Release dates can move.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck after 2026-11-20 (Sunrise opening) and when Netflix dates Scooby-Doo: Origins.

claims.claim: She is in a relationship with her Regretting You and Nimrods co-star Mason Thames, reported as of February 2026 and discussed on air in June 2026.
claims.inference: Thames is a close confidant ('knows every single one of my secrets'), which matters for weighing his testimony and her feedback loop.
claims.alternative: Relationship status changes; never use it as personality evidence.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck for any breakup, engagement or change in public status before publication and at each refresh.

claims.claim: She received the Newport Beach Film Festival's Spotlight Award in October 2026 (reported as October 18).
claims.inference: Context for the October 2026 ET interview in which she described stage fright and not belonging.
claims.alternative: Award confirmed only by the interviewer and unopened fan-news sites; low-stakes metadata.

claims.claim: She attended the March 2026 Academy Awards with Mason Thames and described going to the Oscars as a lifelong dream she 'just got to cross off' her bucket list.
claims.inference: She openly holds conventional recognition goals: in October 2025 she told Collider she wanted 'to go to the Oscars so bad someday'.
claims.alternative: Attending the Oscars is a common actor aspiration; weak evidence for any type.

claims.claim: Across 2025-2026 she repeatedly describes work as the center of her life: 'My job is my life... I don't like to sit still, so I spend my weekends in the studio' (June 2026); 'I don't really go out. I don't party. I don't do anything on the weekends' (June 2026); 'All I've ever wanted is to work... it's what I've dedicated my life to' (March 2026); 'Even whenever I'm off a production, I'm still working' (October 2025).
claims.inference: Work organizes her identity and time to an unusual degree, consistently across interviews and over a year apart.
claims.alternative: A career started at five by a family-run operation, plus promotional settings that reward 'I love my job' answers, could produce this without any particular motive. It fits Three (identity in output), Six (work as security) and Seven (restlessness) alike.

claims.claim: She worked back-to-back through 2025 (Scream 7 pre-production, Five Nights at Freddy's 2, Scream 7, Nimrods, Regretting You, Sunrise on the Reaping), said she had not taken a break 'in years', and told SiriusXM she sleeps little ('I just don't sleep') and leans on espresso and energy drinks on productions.
claims.inference: A costly, repeated choice: exhaustion and no downtime in exchange for continuous work.
claims.alternative: Booking density reflects demand for her, and scheduling is partly outside her control.

claims.claim: She repeatedly says she treats every job as if it could be her last: 'I always treat every job like it could be my last' (HERO, March 2026); 'I treat every project like it could be my last' (L'Officiel, June 2026); 'I treat everything like it could be the last' (SiriusXM, June 2026); she walks 'into every room like... it could be the last job I have' (Who Let Alyssa Out, October 2026).
claims.inference: A recurring scarcity frame: work could vanish at any moment. This supports a security motive (Six) more than pure ambition, though she also presents it as gratitude.
claims.alternative: It may be a polished junket formula for gratitude. Repetition shows it is her own phrase, not that it reflects fear.

claims.claim: She links her extra work to a hostile industry and to a moral guardrail: 'Sometimes I feel like I do extra work because this industry is so cutthroat at times... I wouldn't want to... step on somebody else to make my way up. It scares me, and I don't think I would like myself very much if that's who I became.'
claims.inference: She works harder as protection against a threatening environment, and fears what ambition could turn her into.
claims.alternative: Read as Three: she knows her career drive is strong ('very high importance') and guards against it becoming her whole identity. Read as Two: she fears being selfish. One interview.

claims.claim: She rejects luck framing: 'I'm not manifesting. I am working my butt off. I'm like behind the scenes like trying to finagle everything that I can' (June 2026). Joseph Zada calls her 'a bit of a manifester'.
claims.inference: She wants success understood as the product of her effort and maneuvering.
claims.alternative: Equally compatible with Three (credit for achievement) and Six (control through effort); a reply to a host's prompt.

claims.claim: She lobbies for years for roles in franchises she loves: 'hounding Blumhouse for what feels like 10 years' for Five Nights at Freddy's; 'after this project for so, so long' for Scooby-Doo; 'begging them to hire me' and 'going out for it for ages... so quiet and so secret' for Sunrise on the Reaping.
claims.inference: Persistent, self-directed pursuit of belonging inside beloved fan properties.
claims.alternative: Strategic career-building in a branded-IP era; also fan identity. Persistence itself does not separate types.

claims.claim: Asked by THR (March 2026) whether as a lead she should hold out for leads rather than five-minute parts, she rejected the status frame: 'I don't even see myself that way... If I'm going to be there for five minutes, why not?' She said she had sent Five Nights at Freddy's creators a video offering to 'play a pair of shoes in the background... I would even be your shadow on set. So I'm just a fan.'
claims.inference: Being part of a franchise she loves outranks billing. This counts against a Three reading centered on rank and image, and fits Six (belonging), Seven (fun) or Two.
claims.alternative: Small parts in mega-franchises may be a shrewd visibility strategy, and junket humility rewards this answer. Not yet a defensible discriminator.

claims.claim: She manages scrutiny through preparation: 'So I always get very nervous and try to do my research so I can perform to the best of my abilities without getting in my head about it' (THR). She kept character notebooks and stayed up until about 2 a.m. writing in the book's margins with Zada; she brought Francis Lawrence an annotated book and a notebook of ideas in week one; and she wore Maysilee's braid 'every single day of pre-production to try and convince them. I didn't need to convince them.'
claims.inference: She anticipates resistance and judgment and works to get ahead of them, even when, by her own account, the resistance never came.
claims.alternative: Thorough preparation is standard craft for a book adaptation with an intense fan base. The braid story is told as a joke.

claims.claim: Over roughly a year she repeatedly readied music releases and then pulled them about a week out: 'I kind of like break down and I'm like... the internet's going to hate this like they're all going to hate it... I pull it.' She finally decided to 'rip the band-aid off' with 'Ugly and Rotten' (June 2026).
claims.inference: A costly, repeated choice: fear of public rejection overrode her creative output. L'Officiel confirms she had not released music 'in over a year'.
claims.alternative: Fits Six (anticipatory worst case), Three (fear of public failure) and Two (fear of being disliked) equally. Her filming schedule is a competing explanation she also gives (S02, S15). A single first-person source for the pulling itself.

claims.claim: She says the 2025-2026 virality cycle made her nervous in public for the first time: 'I have never gotten nervous on a carpet or in interviews until now... I was a nervous wreck... Every other week, the internet either loves you or hates you' (March 2026). In June 2026 she added that the internet 'kind of decide when they like you and they don't'.
claims.inference: Shows acute sensitivity to public approval, and dates the onset.
claims.alternative: By her own account the anxiety is recent and circumstantial, triggered by the 2026 virality cycle, which weakens it as evidence of a lifelong core type.

claims.claim: In adult interviews she repeatedly describes self-doubt and not belonging: 'I don't always have that kind of confidence... I'm still every day proving myself' (October 2025); 'Who let me onto this set?... somebody's going to kick me off soon' (December 2025); 'the craziest impostor syndrome' (June 2026); 'I have stage fright... I totally feel like I don't belong... pitching myself even on the days that like I totally don't believe in myself... I still feel like I have a lot to prove' (October 2026).
claims.inference: Persistent insecurity about whether she has earned her place: Six (belonging, doubt) or Three (worth must be proven).
claims.alternative: Self-deprecation is the expected register for a young star on a junket, and some lines are jokes. 'Proving myself' fits Three as well as Six.

claims.claim: Asked when people began seeing her as a leading lady, she said she is trying to adopt that self-view: 'if I view myself in that way then I can try and convince other people to view... myself in that way' (October 2026).
claims.inference: A deliberate image strategy, in which she adopts the self-image others should see. This is the clearest Three-shaped passage in the record.
claims.alternative: One auto-captioned red-carpet answer. It could be ordinary confidence self-talk or counterphobic courage (Six).

claims.claim: She manufactures positive energy on purpose: 'some days I just gaslight myself into being happy or energetic', using a rainbow-dolphin image as 'my energy for the day' (Teen Vogue, November 2025). She tries to be 'positive as much as I can, no matter the circumstance' because 'I have eyes on me and I've had eyes on me my whole life' (October 2026).
claims.inference: Positivity is a chosen discipline tied to being watched and to the people in the room.
claims.alternative: Three (managing affect for performance and image), Seven (reframing toward the positive) and Two (for others) all fit. Publicists reward this.

claims.claim: Teen Vogue's interviewer observed that 'there is little that... Grace can't spin into something good. Rejection is fuel. Disappointment is a sign of desire...', and watched her 'searching for a bright side' when discussing her spinal surgery.
claims.inference: An outside observer saw habitual reframing of negatives, the strongest Seven-shaped evidence in the record.
claims.alternative: One writer, one sitting, framed for a cover headline ('Relentless Optimist'). She also openly narrates pain elsewhere (C18, C20, C38).

claims.claim: She names kindness as her core value: 'I always want to make people feel important and seen. Even sometimes, maybe to a fault. I think that I can be a little overly excited' (November 2025). She says she tries 'to spread kindness and happiness wherever I can and I fail sometimes' (October 2026).
claims.inference: Making others feel seen is how she describes herself. This is the core of the Two alternative.
claims.alternative: A stated value, not an observed cost. Also consistent with a Three or Six who prizes being liked or keeping the group together.

claims.claim: She takes care of colleagues on set. During the Sunrise shoot in Spain she made Zada join dinner with her mother 'every night' when he was too tired, and made him a birthday cake from supermarket sponge cake, strawberries and whipped cream. She brought the Scream 7 stunt team cookies 'every day'. A fellow Scream panelist said she makes cookies with her mother and 'sets the family tone'.
claims.inference: Repeated, concrete caretaking that builds group cohesion: Two (giving) or Six (group 'family').
claims.alternative: Normal collegial warmth on long shoots. The panelist is unidentified.

claims.claim: Joseph Zada, her Sunrise on the Reaping co-star and next-door neighbor for six weeks of the shoot, described her as 'the sweetest person in the world', still 'so excited to meet everyone', and 'somebody who could never stop working'.
claims.inference: Independent of her self-reports on warmth and work rate, though not of the promotional setting.
claims.alternative: A mutual-praise magazine conversation. He observes behavior, not motive.

claims.claim: Mason Thames, her co-star and partner, praised 'her work ethic... how just powerful she is' (October 2025).
claims.inference: Corroborates the work-rate pattern from someone close to her.
claims.alternative: Not independent: promotional and romantically involved.

claims.claim: Her family notices role absorption. Thames and her mother told her 'your personality changes a bit after each of the sets' ('just tired' as Maysilee, 'the bubbliest we've ever seen you' as Daphne). She recalls that as a child playing Christmas Flint 'that was my personality for a year', and says 'I'll go be other people, and then I get home, and I'm me.'
claims.inference: A chameleon quality that the Three reading explains (identity adapts to the role), offset by her own claim of a stable family-anchored self.
claims.alternative: Occupational: actors who start very young often absorb roles. She says she is 'not method'. The Christmas Flint memory is adult retrospection about childhood and is used only as such.

claims.claim: As a 19-year-old executive producer on Regretting You she held back for fear of overstepping ('you never want to overstep your balance or you never want to like step on anybody's toes') until long green-room conversations with Allison Williams and Dave Franco in the last week of production helped her see that 'it's not disrespectful and it's not um overstepping just to give your opinion'.
claims.inference: Deference to hierarchy, and needing permission from trusted seniors before asserting herself: Six- or Two-shaped.
claims.alternative: Ordinary for the youngest producer on a set; she frames it as a gender and age dynamic, not personal anxiety.

claims.claim: She seeks trusted feedback before going public. Thames is her music 'test audience' ('You got to tell me if you actually hate it'), and she calls Octavia Spencer's advice, including a call urging her to take Regretting You, 'formative for me growing up'.
claims.inference: Reliance on a small circle of trusted people for reassurance and direction: Six-shaped.
claims.alternative: Seeking feedback from a partner and a mentor is common and sensible.

claims.claim: She describes herself as a fan who wants to belong to franchise 'families': she snuck into the Scream cast photo op at a convention, followed Matthew Lillard and another original Scream actor around conventions as a fan for 'the past 2 or 3 years', told Lillard about Scooby-Doo before almost anyone, and calls being cast in these franchises getting 'to be a part of these same families'.
claims.inference: Belonging to beloved communities is a repeated pull in her adult choices.
claims.alternative: Genuine fandom and convention culture; the fan persona is also part of her public brand.

claims.claim: She treats casts as family: 'Our little family' (Spain, with Zada and the mothers); 'I have such a nice family off of that film' (Regretting You); texting her cast 'I miss you guys already' after half a day away (June 2026).
claims.inference: Attachment to the group is a stable feature across productions.
claims.alternative: Common among actors on long location shoots, and especially among former child actors.

claims.claim: She expected rejection before her Sunrise casting: 'every time I get fan-casted for a role, I want so bad... and then I don't get it.' When castmates guessed her news she joked, 'You're going to make me lose the job that I don't have... I was so scared' (October 2025).
claims.inference: Anticipatory pessimism about outcomes she wants badly: Six-shaped.
claims.alternative: Told with humor in a junket. A real pattern of losing fan-cast roles would justify the caution.

claims.claim: She separates acting from music: 'In acting, I'm telling other people's stories. In music, I get to tell my own. It's a lot scarier... I get to be a lot angrier or messier... When I'm singing, I don't want to feel like I'm putting on another identity, since that's what I do for work already' (June 2026).
claims.inference: She is aware that her work involves wearing identities and protects one space from that. This complicates a simple Three reading.
claims.alternative: Common artist framing; also hints at a Four-like authenticity concern the evidence does not otherwise support.

claims.claim: She notes a contrast between a 'very like bubbly personality' and 'bright like poppy aesthetic' and her love of horror, heavy metal and 'dark romance' (October 2025). She shares the horror and metal tastes with her father.
claims.inference: The persona and the private tastes diverge, which no leading type neatly explains.
claims.alternative: Taste is weak personality evidence.

claims.claim: She avoids cursing: she says she 'kind of got like bullied into' cursing when younger, hates it, and uses 'jeepers' instead (June 2026; March 2026).
claims.inference: A personal standard she holds against peer pressure. Unexplained by the leading types.
claims.alternative: Small and possibly image-conscious; her reasons are not given in depth.

claims.claim: She reframes past pain as formative: 'I can't look back and regret what I've done in the past... it's made you who you are today' (October 2025). Of eight months' training for a film that was then shelved, she said, 'everything happens for a reason. I'm so glad I did it' (November 2025).
claims.inference: Habitual positive reframing, supporting the Seven and Three alternatives.
claims.alternative: Theme-of-the-movie answer for Regretting You; reframing after a hard recovery is common.

claims.claim: Looking back as an adult, she describes poor body image as a younger teenager, her 2022 spinal surgery as 'the hardest thing I've ever done' followed by greater confidence, and fashion as something that moved from 'anxiety' to 'healing'.
claims.inference: Context for her current confidence and style; not type evidence.
claims.alternative: Sensitive health and minor-era material. Use only her adult framing, and omit the minor-era body rumor unless strictly necessary.

claims.claim: She describes her job as dependent on being liked: 'The whole basis of my job is hoping that people like me and that people want to hire me' and 'your whole thing is to make people like you' (November 2025). She also says she cannot control what is out there of her and uses social media to show 'here's me'.
claims.inference: Approval sensitivity is explicit, but she attributes it to the profession.
claims.alternative: Occupational truth for any actor; it does not separate Two, Three and Six.

claims.claim: As an adult she recalls being 'really sad cuz I'd worked really hard on it' when a 2016 carpet interviewer assumed she was there for her mother: 'Man, like I just want to be an actress.'
claims.inference: Wanting her work recognized is an early and enduring theme in her own telling.
claims.alternative: A comic retelling of a childhood memory. It must not be used to type the child.

claims.claim: Provisional leading read, held at low confidence: Type 6. Work, preparation and belonging to cast and fan 'families' seem to protect her against a scrutiny she expects to turn on her: every job could be her last, she prepares to pre-empt resistance, pulls releases she fears will be hated, and asks trusted people for permission and feedback.
claims.inference: Explains the anxiety, preparation, deference and group attachment better than the alternatives do.
claims.alternative: Three explains the output, image-awareness and chameleon quality. Two explains the caretaking. Seven explains the deliberate joy and reframing. Her bubbly, trusting public register is not typical Six.

claims.claim: Strongest alternative: Type 3. Her identity has been built around continuous work since age five. She talks about proving herself, credits effort over luck, consciously projects a self-image so others will adopt it, manufactures energy for the room, and shifts personality with roles.
claims.inference: Explains the relentless output and the image management directly.
claims.alternative: Her rejection of rank (C16), her open confessions of insecurity and her fan identity sit awkwardly with a Three focused on image.

claims.claim: Types 2 and 7 remain live. Two rests on her stated core value of making people feel 'important and seen... to a fault' and on repeated caretaking (C24, C25). Seven rests on her self-generated joy, 'I can't sit still', and a journalist's observation that she spins everything into something good (C22, C23, C37).
claims.inference: No current evidence rules either out.
claims.alternative: Two is weakened by her putting work ahead of social life (C10). Seven is weakened by her open dwelling on fear, pain and doubt (C18, C20, C38).

type_hypothesis.against: Several things cut against a Six reading. Her default public register is high, bubbly enthusiasm and deliberate positivity (C22, C23, C35), with little of the suspicion, testing of authority or worst-case talk about people that Six usually shows; she lobbies studios and directors for years rather than doubting them (C15). By her own account she 'never' got nervous on a carpet in nearly 15 years until the 2026 virality cycle (C19), so some of the anxiety is recent and circumstantial. Her work drive reads at least as much like identity and proving (C10, C11, C14, C20, C21) as like security. Her stated core value is making people feel 'important and seen... to a fault' (C24), a Two signature, and a Teen Vogue interviewer saw her turn everything into something good (C23), a Seven-like habit. Nearly every source is promotional, and much of the self-doubt is junket self-deprecation the format rewards.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 3: Work has organized her identity since she was five ('My job is my life'; 'All I've ever wanted is to work'; C10, C11). She talks about having 'a lot to prove' (C20), credits effort and behind-the-scenes 'finagling' over luck (C14), and describes a conscious strategy of adopting a self-image so that others will adopt it ('if I view myself in that way then I can try and convince other people', C21). She manufactures energy for the room ('gaslight myself into being happy or energetic', C22), her partner and mother see her personality shift with each role (C28), she calls being liked 'the whole basis of my job' (C39), and she fears public rejection enough to pull finished songs (C18). This explains the relentless output, the image-awareness and the chameleon quality more directly than Six does.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: No defensible discriminator yet. The best candidate is rank versus belonging. Asked by THR in March 2026 whether a lead actor should hold out for leads, she rejected the status frame ('I don't even see myself that way') and described offering to 'play a pair of shoes in the background' to get into a franchise she loves (C16). That points away from Three, but branded-IP career economics and junket humility weaken it, and it does not separate Six from Seven or Two. The second candidate, what she does with self-doubt, splits evenly: preparation, trusted feedback and asking permission (C17, C29, C30) read Six, while projecting a chosen self-image and manufacturing energy (C21, C22) read Three. Pulling releases for fear of hate (C18) fits Six, Three and Two equally. A real discriminator needs adult, non-promotional evidence of how she handles a setback, or a choice between belonging and advancement.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Her role absorption ('your personality changes a bit after each of the sets', C28) alongside her insistence that music is where she refuses to 'put on another identity' (C34). Her firm aversion to cursing (C36). The darker tastes (metal, horror, angry diary-based songs) beneath a pink, bubbly persona (C35). The tension between 'I don't want to get too ambitious' (S03) and 'I put my career at very high importance' (C13). How much of the work rate and the mother-managed structure (C02, C03) is a family business set in early childhood rather than temperament.
